CT-368 — Phase 1 and Phase 2¶

Late Delivery Risk Prediction in E-Commerce Logistics¶

Dataset: E-Commerce Delivery & Shipping Data 2026 (Kaggle), 50,000 orders × 30 columns.

Name Roll number
Danyal Abbas CT-24084

Problem. Predict, before an order ships, whether it will miss its promised delivery date. Target late_delivery (Yes/No) is binary, so this is a classification problem.

All randomness uses random_state=42. The raw file is never modified.

1. Features and target¶

Rows: one order each. Columns: 30, in three groups.

Used as features (17) — all known before the parcel ships:

Column Meaning
order_date date the order was placed
customer_segment Consumer / Small Business / Enterprise / Premium
customer_country destination country (17)
warehouse_city city the order ships from (10)
product_category product department (12)
product_weight_kg parcel weight, 0.1–52 kg
order_value_usd order value, $10–$3,531
shipping_method Same Day / Express / Standard / Economy / International
carrier logistics partner (8)
distance_km warehouse-to-customer distance
promised_delivery_days delivery promise, 0–15 days
shipping_cost_usd freight charge
package_size Small / Medium / Large / Oversized
payment_method 6 payment types
order_priority Low / Normal / High / Urgent
weather_condition Clear / Cloudy / Rain / Snow / Storm / Extreme Heat
warehouse_processing_hours pick-and-pack time, 1–48 h

Target (1): late_delivery — Yes if the order missed its promise (56.3% of rows).

Dropped as identifiers (4): order_id, customer_id (arbitrary codes), customer_city (99 levels, redundant with country), warehouse_id (1:1 with warehouse_city).

Dropped as leakage (8) — recorded after delivery, so unusable at prediction time: actual_delivery_days, delivery_delay_days, delivery_status, tracking_status, customer_rating, return_requested, return_reason, delivery_attempts. §2 shows why this matters.

Cleaning also creates one extra input, shipping_cost_capped, a 0/1 flag for the 658 orders whose freight charge was capped at $500.

3. Cleaning¶

Change Why
Remove duplicates none exist (0 rows removed)
order_date → datetime stored as text
Drop 4 identifier columns codes, not measurements
Drop 8 leakage columns unknown at prediction time
Add shipping_cost_capped marks the 658 censored costs instead of deleting them
Keep outliers real orders, no effect on the late rate

4. Train / test split¶

80/20, stratified so both halves keep the 56.3% late rate. random_state=42. Splitting before any imputation or scaling is what prevents leakage from the test set.

In [9]:
FEATURES = [c for c in clean.columns if c != "late_delivery"]
X = clean[FEATURES].copy()
y = clean["late_delivery"].map({"No": 0, "Yes": 1})

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y)

print(f"train {X_train.shape}, test {X_test.shape}")
print(f"late rate — train {y_train.mean()*100:.2f}%, test {y_test.mean()*100:.2f}%")

train (40000, 18), test (10000, 18)
late rate — train 56.33%, test 56.32%

5. Preprocessing and feature selection¶

Three engineered features, all row-wise:

  • weather_severity — Clear 0 → Snow 5, because the risk rises in that order.
  • priority_rank — Urgent 0 → Low 3.
  • distance_per_promised_day — how much ground must be covered per promised day.

order_date is dropped rather than split into month/day: the monthly late rate stays between 55.5% and 57.7% across the year, so there is no seasonality to capture.

Then a pipeline: median-impute + scale the numerics, most-frequent-impute + one-hot the categories, select the 15 best encoded columns by mutual information, and fit logistic regression. The pipeline is fitted on the training rows only.

In [10]:
WEATHER = {"Clear": 0, "Cloudy": 1, "Extreme Heat": 2, "Rain": 3, "Storm": 4, "Snow": 5}
PRIORITY = {"Urgent": 0, "High": 1, "Normal": 2, "Low": 3}


def add_features(frame):
    f = frame.copy()
    f["weather_severity"] = f["weather_condition"].map(WEATHER)
    f["priority_rank"] = f["order_priority"].map(PRIORITY)
    f["distance_per_promised_day"] = f["distance_km"] / f["promised_delivery_days"].clip(lower=1)
    return f.drop(columns=["order_date"])


def mi_score(X, y):
    # Seeded so SelectKBest picks the same 15 columns on every run.
    return mutual_info_classif(X, y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)


X_train = add_features(X_train)
X_test = add_features(X_test)

num_cols = X_train.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist()
cat_cols = X_train.select_dtypes("object").columns.tolist()
print(f"{len(num_cols)} numeric, {len(cat_cols)} categorical")

10 numeric, 10 categorical
In [11]:
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]), cat_cols),
])

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", prep),
    ("select", SelectKBest(mi_score, k=15)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])

pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
prob = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

results = pd.DataFrame([{
    "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, pred),
    "Precision": precision_score(y_test, pred),
    "Recall": recall_score(y_test, pred),
    "F1": f1_score(y_test, pred),
    "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, prob),
}]).round(3)
results

6. Class imbalance¶

56.3% late vs 43.7% on-time — a 1.3:1 ratio, which is mild. No resampling is needed, but class weights are worth checking.

In [13]:
weighted = Pipeline([
    ("prep", prep),
    ("select", SelectKBest(mi_score, k=15)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced",
                                 random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
])
weighted.fit(X_train, y_train)
prob_w = weighted.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
pred_w = weighted.predict(X_test)

compare = pd.DataFrame([
    ["No weighting", accuracy_score(y_test, pred), precision_score(y_test, pred),
     recall_score(y_test, pred), roc_auc_score(y_test, prob)],
    ["class_weight=balanced", accuracy_score(y_test, pred_w), precision_score(y_test, pred_w),
     recall_score(y_test, pred_w), roc_auc_score(y_test, prob_w)],
], columns=["Model", "Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "ROC-AUC"]).round(3)

Class weighting barely changes ROC-AUC and lowers recall on late orders, so the plain model is kept. Nothing here justifies SMOTE at a 1.3:1 ratio.

7. Problem and method¶

Problem type: classification. The target late_delivery is binary, so this is not a regression problem and the regression metrics named in the brief — MAE, MSE, RMSE and R² — do not apply here. The metrics that do apply are accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and the confusion matrix, and all six are reported in §9 for every model.

What is predicted. Whether an order that has just been accepted will miss its promised delivery date. The prediction is made at order time, from pre-dispatch information only.

Inputs. The 17 features listed in §1, minus order_date (dropped in §5), plus shipping_cost_capped from §3 and the three engineered features from §5 — 20 model inputs in total, all passed through the same preprocessing pipeline.

Why machine learning is suitable.

  1. The signal is multivariate and interacting. §1 showed that weather, priority and distance compound (storm at 5,000+ km was 100% late, clear under 1,000 km was 16.7%), so a hand-written rule would need a branch for every combination.
  2. There are 40,000 training orders — enough to estimate that structure without memorising it.
  3. The output is a probability per order, which can be ranked: the fulfilment team acts on the riskiest slice rather than a single yes/no.
  4. The relationship is stable over time, so a model fitted on part of the data generalises to the rest (§9 and §11 measure exactly that).

Protocol, and how leakage is avoided.

Step Data used
Imputation, scaling, one-hot encoding, feature selection fitted inside the pipeline, so re-fitted from scratch on every CV fold and on the final fit
Cross-validation X_train only — 5-fold StratifiedKFold(shuffle=True, random_state=42)
Hyperparameter search X_train only, using the same CV folds
Model selection CV score on X_train only
Test set used once, in §11, after every decision is fixed

Because the selector and the scaler live inside the pipeline, a fold's validation rows never contribute to a median, a mean, the list of categories, or the feature ranking. The test set is untouched until the final evaluation.

8. Training and cross-validation¶

Four models from two families. Depth and leaf limits on the trees are deliberate — an unrestricted tree reaches 100% training accuracy on 40,000 rows in seconds, which §11 quantifies.

Model How it works Why it is here
Logistic regression Fits one weighted sum of the inputs and passes it through the logistic function, giving a linear decision boundary. The standard baseline: fast, interpretable, and dependent on scaling — so it also tests the preprocessing.
Decision tree Recursively splits the data at the single most informative threshold, producing an if/else rule set. Fully interpretable and scale-free, but prone to overfitting — a useful contrast.
Random forest Fits many trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then averages their votes. Keeps the tree's non-linearity while averaging away its variance.
Gradient boosting Fits trees sequentially, each correcting the error left by the previous ensemble. Usually the strongest learner on tabular data of this size.

Each model is wrapped in the same Pipeline, so the comparison is fair: same imputation, same encoding, same 15 selected features, same folds.

In [16]:
MODELS = {
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=8, min_samples_leaf=20,
                                           random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5,
                                            n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.1,
                                                        random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}


def build(model):
    return Pipeline([
        ("prep", prep),
        ("select", SelectKBest(mi_score, k=15)),
        ("model", model),
    ])


cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
scoring = {"accuracy": "accuracy", "precision": "precision", "recall": "recall",
           "f1": "f1", "roc_auc": "roc_auc"}

cv_rows, fitted, train_auc = [], {}, {}
for name, model in MODELS.items():
    candidate = build(model)
    scores = cross_validate(candidate, X_train, y_train, cv=cv,
                            scoring=scoring, n_jobs=-1)
    candidate.fit(X_train, y_train)
    fitted[name] = candidate
    train_auc[name] = roc_auc_score(y_train, candidate.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
    cv_rows.append({"Model": name,
                    **{k: scores[f"test_{k}"].mean() for k in scoring},
                    "ROC-AUC std": scores["test_roc_auc"].std()})

cv_table = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).set_index("Model").round(3)
cv_table

The cross-validated ranking is the one used to choose the model, because it is measured on training data that the model did not see inside each fold.

9. Evaluation and comparison¶

Why these metrics. The classes are close to balanced (56.3% late), so accuracy is meaningful, but on its own it hides which mistakes are being made. Precision and recall separate the two error types (false alarms versus missed late orders), F1 summarises them, and ROC-AUC measures ranking quality independently of the 0.5 threshold — which matters because the operating threshold is a business decision, not a property of the model. The confusion matrix shows the actual counts behind all of it.

In [17]:
test_rows, test_prob, test_pred = [], {}, {}
for name, model in fitted.items():
    p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    y_hat = model.predict(X_test)
    test_prob[name], test_pred[name] = p, y_hat
    test_rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Test accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_hat),
        "Test precision": precision_score(y_test, y_hat),
        "Test recall": recall_score(y_test, y_hat),
        "Test F1": f1_score(y_test, y_hat),
        "Test ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, p),
    })

test_table = pd.DataFrame(test_rows).set_index("Model").round(3)

comparison = cv_table[["accuracy", "f1", "roc_auc"]].rename(
    columns={"accuracy": "CV accuracy", "f1": "CV F1", "roc_auc": "CV ROC-AUC"})
comparison = comparison.join(test_table)
comparison.round(3)

10. Hyperparameter tuning¶

Gradient boosting is tuned, because it has the most consequential knobs — how fast it learns and how complex each tree may be — and it was the strongest model before tuning. Two parameters, four combinations, the same 5 folds, scoring on ROC-AUC:

  • learning_rate — how much each new tree contributes. Too high underfits nothing but overfits the training rows; too low needs more trees.
  • max_leaf_nodes — the maximum number of leaves per tree, i.e. how deep an interaction the ensemble can represent.

GridSearchCV refits the whole pipeline (including imputation, encoding and selection) for every combination and every fold, so the search is honest.

In [21]:
param_grid = {
    "model__learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1],
    "model__max_leaf_nodes": [15, 31],
}

search = GridSearchCV(
    build(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
    param_grid, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

The tuning surface is flat: the four configurations differ by a few thousandths of an AUC point, and the error bars overlap. That is the expected result when a model is already close to the information ceiling of its features — it also means the choice of hyperparameters is not where the remaining performance lies.

11. Results and discussion¶

11.1 Best and worst models¶

Best: gradient boosting, first on every metric — CV ROC-AUC 0.896, test ROC-AUC 0.898, test F1 0.828. Worst: logistic regression, at 0.881 CV and 0.882 test.

The decision tree (0.889 CV / 0.891 test) and the random forest (0.890 CV / 0.889 test) sit between them and are effectively tied: a 0.001 difference changes sign between the two evaluation sets, which is what noise looks like at this sample size. That tie is itself informative. With max_depth=8 and 20 orders per leaf the single tree is already regularised, and the extra machinery of 200 averaged trees buys nothing on a signal that is mostly additive with one strong interaction.

The two ends of the table are explainable:

  • Gradient boosting wins because it combines the two things this problem needs — a non-linear split (so weather × distance needs no hand-built feature) and sequential correction of residual error (so rare high-risk cells are fitted harder on later trees).
  • Logistic regression loses because its boundary is linear in the selected features. It sees weather_severity and distance_km separately, so it must average over their interaction, exactly the weakness §1.7 predicted. Its train and CV scores are also identical (0.881 / 0.881), which means it is not overfitting — it is limited by its functional form (high bias), not by variance.

11.2 Overfitting and underfitting¶

The gap between the training score and the cross-validated score is the diagnostic. A large positive gap is overfitting; a low score everywhere is underfitting.

  • The random forest has by far the largest gap: 0.961 on training data against 0.890 in cross-validation, a 0.071 drop. Averaging 200 trees controls the variance of a prediction but does not stop the individual trees from memorising their bootstrap samples, so the training score stays optimistic. Crucially, its CV and test scores agree (0.890 vs 0.889), so the gap is a training-score artefact, not a generalisation failure.
  • Decision tree 0.012, gradient boosting 0.010, logistic regression −0.000. The depth and leaf limits keep the single tree in check, and boosting's sequential fitting with 200 rounds does not run away either.
  • Nothing here shows underfitting: every model beats the 0.563 majority-class baseline by a wide margin, and the CV scores are stable across folds (standard deviation 0.003 for all four).
  • The most reassuring pattern in the comparison table is this: for every model, the test ROC-AUC is within 0.002 of the CV ROC-AUC. The cross-validation estimate was therefore honest, not optimistic, which is the property that makes the final §11.4 result trustworthy.

11.3 Did tuning help?¶

Marginally, and honestly so. The best configuration lowers the learning rate from 0.10 to 0.05 and shrinks each tree from 31 to 15 leaves. That moves CV ROC-AUC from 0.8964 to 0.8976 (+0.0012); the test ROC-AUC is unchanged at 0.898 and F1 actually slips from 0.828 to 0.827.

So tuning bought a gain smaller than the fold-to-fold standard deviation (0.003). That is a real finding rather than a disappointment: when a model is limited by its features and not by its settings, tuning cannot buy much. The practical value of the search here is negative — four configurations × five folds is twenty extra fits for no measurable improvement — which is itself a useful result to report.

The tuned model is still the one carried forward, because it is at least as good on every metric and its CV score is the highest of the four configurations.

11.4 Final model on the test set¶

The tuned gradient-boosting pipeline is evaluated once on the 10,000 held-out orders. Its test ROC-AUC is within a few thousandths of its cross-validated score, which is the check that matters: the CV estimate was not optimistic, so the model is not overfitted to the training data and the selection procedure did not leak.

11.5 Limitations¶

  • One year of orders. The monthly late rate barely moves (55.5–57.7%), so there is no seasonality to learn and no year-over-year drift to measure. The reported scores describe this 2026 sample; a later period could shift them.
  • The promise is partly a restatement of the distance. promised_delivery_days correlates 0.93 with actual_delivery_days, so the model partly learns "long promise → late". That is operationally true, but it is a weaker causal story than "weather causes delay".
  • No cost matrix. Precision and recall are reported separately rather than combined into a business loss, because nothing in the data prices a false alarm against a missed late order. The 0.5 threshold is therefore a default, not an optimum.
  • A single split. The test set is one random 20% sample. A repeated nested CV would give tighter confidence intervals on the final score.
  • Only four models and one tuned. The comparison is wide, not exhaustive; gradient boosting was tuned but the others were left at sensible defaults.

12. Conclusion¶

What the project set out to do. Predict, at order time, whether an e-commerce order will miss its promised delivery date, using only information available before the parcel ships.

What was built. Phase 1 cleaned the 50,000-row dataset, diagnosed and removed eight post-outcome leakage columns, split the data 80/20 with stratification, and built a preprocessing pipeline of median imputation, scaling, one-hot encoding and mutual-information feature selection. Phase 2 compared four models under identical 5-fold cross-validation, tuned the strongest one, and evaluated it once on the held-out test set.

What was found.

  1. Weather and priority drive lateness. Snow is 93.5% late against 35.0% for clear conditions; low-priority orders are 81.7% late against 25.7% for urgent ones.
  2. Distance matters and money does not. The late rate rises from 38.5% below 1,000 km to 82.8% above 5,000 km, while order value is flat across its whole range (r = −0.001).
  3. The biggest data risk was leakage, not missing data. Eight columns describe the finished delivery; delivery_delay_days alone reproduces the target perfectly (AUC 1.0000). Removing them is what makes the reported 0.88–0.89 range credible.
  4. Outliers were real orders. The IQR rule flags 11.9% of rows holding 55.7% of revenue, with the same late rate as the rest — deleting them would have destroyed the business signal.
  5. Model choice matters less than the features. All four models land between 0.881 and 0.898 ROC-AUC, tuning moves the best one by 0.001, and the ordering — boosting > forest ≈ single tree > logistic regression — is exactly what their functional forms predict: the ensembles can represent the interaction, the linear model cannot.

Objectives achieved. The tuned gradient-boosting pipeline ranks orders by lateness risk at 0.898 ROC-AUC on unseen data (0.804 accuracy, 0.828 F1), well above the 0.563 majority-class baseline, using only pre-dispatch information and a pipeline that cannot leak test data. The remaining error is dominated by cases whose causes are not in the dataset (carrier execution, traffic, local disruptions), which is where further work would start.
